{{short description|Symbol used in mathematics and typography}}
[[Image:Halmos symbols.svg|frame|right|Various forms of the end-of-proof symbol]]
In mathematics, the '''tombstone''', '''halmos''', '''end-of-proof''', or '''Q.E.D.''' symbol "∎" (or "□") is a symbol used to denote the end of a [[Mathematical proof|proof]], in place of the traditional abbreviation "Q.E.D."  for the Latin phrase "''[[Q.E.D.|quod erat demonstrandum]]''". It is inspired by the [[Typography|typographic]] practice of ''[[wikt:end mark|end marks]]'', an element that marks the end of an article.{{r|h1}}<ref>{{cite web |last1=Felici |first1=James |title=The complete manual of typography : a guide to setting perfect type |url=https://archive.org/details/completemanualof0000feli/page/226 |publisher=Berkeley, CA : Peachpit Press |date=2003}}</ref>

In [[Unicode]], it is represented as character {{unichar|220E|End of Proof|html=}}. Its graphic form varies, as it may be a hollow or filled rectangle or square.

In [[AMS-LaTeX]], the symbol is automatically appended at the end of a proof environment <code>\begin{proof}</code> ... <code>\end{proof}</code>. It can also be obtained from the commands <code>\qedsymbol</code>, <code>\qedhere</code> or <code>\qed</code> (the latter causes the symbol to be right aligned).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/LaTeX/Theorems|title=LaTeX/Theorems - Wikibooks, open books for an open world|website=en.wikibooks.org|access-date=2019-11-05}}</ref>

It is sometimes called a "Halmos finality symbol" or "halmos" after the mathematician [[Paul Halmos]], who first used it in a mathematical context in 1950.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Halmos |first1=Paul R. |url=https://archive.org/details/measuretheory00halm/page/22 |title=Measure theory |date=1950 |publisher=Van Nostrand |isbn=0387900888 |location=New York |pages=[https://archive.org/details/measuretheory00halm/page/22 22] |oclc=529634 |url-access=registration}}</ref> He got the idea of using it from seeing [[wikt:end mark|end marks]] in [[magazine]]s, that is, [[typography|typographic]] signs that indicate the end of an article. In his memoir ''I Want to Be a Mathematician'', he wrote the following:<ref name="h1">Paul R. Halmos, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=7VblBwAAQBAJ&q=tombstone&pg=PA3 I Want to Be a Mathematician: An Automathography]'', 1985, p. 403.</ref>
{{quote|The symbol is definitely not my invention&nbsp;– it appeared in popular magazines (not mathematical ones) before I adopted it, but, once again, I seem to have introduced it into mathematics. It is the symbol that sometimes looks like ▯, and is used to indicate an end, usually the end of a proof. It is most frequently called the 'tombstone', but at least one generous author referred to it as the 'halmos'.}}
